data.data-is-any#Data is any:
Every data argument accepts []float64, []float32, []int, []int32, []int64, a scalar, or a *ndarray.Array of any of ndarray’s thirteen dtypes (converted with AsType(Float64), flattened in row-major order; 2-D arrays for Imshow and contours, 3-D (rows, cols, 3|4) arrays as RGB(A) images, uint8 taken as bytes).
A type that cannot be plotted panics, as does a length mismatch. Both are programming errors, exactly as an index out of range is, and returning an error from every Plot call would make every notebook cell three lines longer for a failure that is never handled.
data.figure-subplots-axes#Figure, Subplots, A: fig, axs := plot.Subplots(2, 3) // a 2 x 3 grid: axs is a [][]*plot.Axes ax := axs[1][0] // second row, first column fig := plot.NewFigure(plot.FigSize(6.4, 4.8), plot.DPI(100)) grid := fig.Subplots(1, 2) // the same, on an existing figure inset := fig.AddAxes(0.6, 0.6, 0.25, 0.25) // left, bottom, width, height, in figure fractions plot.Subplots(rows, cols, ...FigOption) returns the figure and a [][]*Axes, always two-dimensional (matplotlib’s squeeze=False). Plot types are Axes methods named as in matplotlib: Plot, Scatter, Bar, Barh, Hist, FillBetween, ErrorBar, Imshow, Contour, Contourf, Axhline, Axvline, Text, Annotate, Legend, SetXLim, SetYScale, TwinX… See plot types. Figure.TightLayout() is matplotlib’s tight_layout, ported. It reports false, changing nothing, when the decorations cannot fit, as matplotlib then warns and does nothing.
data.keyword-arguments-become-options#Keyword:
matplotlib’s keyword arguments become functional options:
ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Color("C1"), plot.LineStyle("--"), plot.Label("data")) is ax.plot(x, y, color="C1", linestyle="--", label="data"). Go has no keywords, and a struct per method would multiply types without adding safety. Each method documents the options it honours; an option a method does not use is ignored.
option matplotlib keyword Color, Colors, FaceColor, EdgeColor, Alpha color, a list of colours, facecolor, edgecolor, alpha LineStyle, LineWidth, Marker, MarkerSize, MarkerEdgeWidth linestyle, linewidth, marker, markersize, markeredgewidth Label, ZOrder, Clip label, zorder, clip_on Width, Bottom, Align bar’s width, bottom, align Bins, BinEdges, Density hist’s bins (a count, or edges), density XErr, YErr, CapSize, ErrorColor errorbar’s xerr, yerr, capsize, ecolor Where fill_between’s where Sizes, CValues scatter’s s and c Cmap, Vmin, Vmax, LogNorm cmap, vmin, vmax, norm=LogNorm() Extent, Origin, Aspect imshow’s extent, origin, aspect Levels, NLevels contour’s levels (a list, or a count) FontSize, HA, VA, Rotation, Arrow fontsize, ha, va, rotation, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->") Loc legend’s loc
data.mappables-and-colorbars#Mappables and co:
Imshow, Scatter with CValues, Contour and Contourf return a *Mappable (a colormap and a norm). Figure.Colorbar(m, ax) draws it, taking its space from ax exactly as fig.colorbar(m, ax=ax) does, and returns the colorbar’s Axes, whose label can be set:
m := ax.Imshow(z, plot.Cmap("viridis")) fig.Colorbar(m, ax).SetYLabel("height (m)")
data.output#Output: method writes SavePNG(w io.Writer) error an anti-aliased raster SaveSVG(w io.Writer) error vector SVG: paths, clip paths, images embedded as PNG, as matplotlib’s SVG backend does with svg.fonttype = "path"; text is drawn as outlines, so no font is needed to show it Display() map[string][]byte the notebook contract: image/svg+xml and image/png
data.packages#Packages: package what it does plot Figure, Axes and every plot type; layout, autoscaling, legend, colorbar ticker tick locations and labels: AutoLocator (MaxNLocator), ScalarFormatter, LogLocator, LogFormatterSciNotation colors colour parsing, the tab10 cycle, eight colormaps, Normalize and LogNorm contour marching squares: iso-lines and filled bands on a rectangular grid render the drawing seam: a Renderer interface, a raster back-end and an SVG back-end text strings to glyph outlines: DejaVu Sans for text, go-tex/math for TeX The full reference is on pkg.go.dev.
data.shaped-by-what-notebooks-call#Shaped by:
go-plot is the plotting library of a Go notebook ecosystem built on go-ndarray. Its API was chosen from a measurement, not a preference.
A census of 339 scientific notebooks (measured for this ecosystem) ranks plotting first among the things that keep them from moving to Go, and gives the share of notebooks using each call:
call notebooks go-plot pyplot.subplots 62 % plot.Subplots Axes.plot 56 % Axes.Plot pyplot.show 52 % Figure.Display, called by the notebook Axes.set_xlabel 47 % Axes.SetXLabel Axes.legend 46 % Axes.Legend, with matplotlib’s location names and "best" Axes.set_ylabel 45 % Axes.SetYLabel Axes.set_title 37 % Axes.SetTitle pyplot.figure 27 % plot.NewFigure tight_layout 27 % Figure.TightLayout module-level pyplot.plot/xlabel/ylabel about 22 % not provided (below) Axes.set_ylim 21 % Axes.SetYLim Axes.axhline 20 % Axes.Axhline Most notebooks write fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(...). So go-plot is the object-oriented API, and every one of those operations exists under the same name.
The module-level, state-machine functions are deliberately not provided. plt.plot and plt.xlabel act on a hidden “current” Axes. They are the minority form, and hidden global state is what a Go notebook kernel running cells concurrently should not have.
data.text-is-a-seam#Text is a seam: Figure.Text is a text.Renderer (Layout(s, size), LineMetrics(size)). The default sets plain text in DejaVu Sans (matplotlib’s default font, from go-opentype/fonts) and TeX between dollar signs with go-tex/math. Replacing the renderer changes the fonts of the whole figure. See TeX labels.

data: What is equal, and how it is checked, is on Exactness. This page is the rest.
data.annotate#Annotate: Annotate draws arrowstyle="->" only, shrunk 2 points at both ends.
data.contours#Contours: Contours are marching squares with the saddle resolved by the cell mean, not contourpy’s serial algorithm (corner_mask, chunking): levels and colours are matplotlib’s, line vertices differ slightly. Filled bands are drawn per grid cell.
data.images#Images: Images are resampled nearest-neighbour when enlarged and box-averaged when reduced; matplotlib’s default (interpolation="auto", antialiased resampling in data space) differs when an image is shown smaller than its resolution, or less than three times enlarged.
data.legend-best#Legend “best”: "best" counts the vertices, segments, boxes and scatter points under each of the nine candidate positions and takes the first with none, else the least; matplotlib’s badness also weights offsets and is computed in display space with a pad. Usually the same place; not always.
data.math-text-is-tex-not-mathtext#Math text: $...$ is typeset by go-tex/math with STIX Two Math — real TeX layout (fractions, radicals, big operators, limits, matrices, \left...\right), which matplotlib’s mathtext only approximates. The exception is \mathdefault{...}, what matplotlib’s tick formatters emit: it is set in DejaVu Sans with mathtext’s own superscript rules, so tick labels match matplotlib’s look and position. See TeX labels.
data.no-module-level-pyplot#No module-level p: plt.plot, plt.xlabel and the other functions acting on a hidden current Axes are not provided, by design: see the API.
data.not-in-v0#Not in v0: suptitle, and TightLayout with explicit pads or rect; symlog, logit and date axes; minor ticks on linear axes (off by default in matplotlib too) and AutoMinorLocator; constrained_layout; subplots sharing; hatching; boxplot, violin, quiver, stem, step, pcolormesh, 3-D; colorbar extend and discrete norms; image interpolation other than nearest; Text bounding boxes; legend columns, titles and bbox_to_anchor; native and browser windows (go-widgets/window); PDF output.
data.pie#Pie:
Pie is ax.pie with matplotlib’s defaults. It differs in six places:
The refusals (negative, NaN, infinite, all zero) are returned as ErrPieNegative, ErrPieNonFinite and ErrPieZero, not raised. A sum of sizes that overflows is taken after scaling, where matplotlib draws every wedge empty. AutoPct takes Go format verbs ("%1.1f%%" works in both; Python’s %d is Go’s %.0f). labeldistance=None is LabelDistance(math.NaN()). There is no shadow, no hatch and no frame=True. Donut, PlainText (labels never reach TeX) and SpreadLabels (labels of thin wedges moved apart, with leader lines) are go-plot’s own.
data.strokes#Strokes: Anti-aliasing is go-gfx’s, not Agg’s; widths, caps, joins and dashes are matplotlib’s. Pixel snapping follows matplotlib’s rule (odd widths at pixel centres, even at edges) for paths made of horizontal and vertical segments. Strokes of more than 512 segments are drawn in pieces and get round ends (see performance).
data.svg#SVG:
The SVG carries the same geometry but not matplotlib’s document structure, ids or metadata.
Since v0.2.0 the SVG can be inlined in an HTML page served under a strict Content-Security-Policy:
Paint is in presentation attributes (fill="…"), not style="…", which a style-src without 'unsafe-inline' would drop. There is no script and no event attribute. No reference leaves the document. Text is glyph outlines, so no label can become markup. A clip’s id is derived from its rectangle, so two figures inlined in one page cannot clip each other. The one data: URI is an Imshow image.
data.text#Text: Glyphs are filled outlines (go-gfx coverage), not FreeType’s hinted rasterisation with matplotlib’s text antialiasing, so the pixels of text differ, and a string’s box is its advance where matplotlib’s is FreeType’s hinted box (up to a few pixels wider on long labels). Positions are matplotlib’s (Text._get_layout: line metrics from the OS/2 table, alignment, rotation, anchoring), and like Agg the pen is put on a whole pixel. Kerning comes from DejaVu’s GPOS/kern tables through go-opentype.

data:
go-plot’s model and defaults are matplotlib’s so that a figure can be checked against matplotlib’s rendering of the same figure, not only look like it.
All fixtures are generated by scripts in tools/ from matplotlib itself (3.11.2), committed, //go:embed-ded in the tests, and compared exactly unless stated.
data.algorithms#Algorithms: what how it is checked Histogram binning NumPy’s algorithm (equal bins by arithmetic, corrected against the edges; explicit edges by searchsorted). Contour levels ContourSet._autolev (MaxNLocator(n+1, min_n_ticks=1), trimmed). Dense lines matplotlib’s PathSimplifier (threshold 1/9 pixel), ported from path_converters.h.
data.colours#Colours: what how it is checked Colormaps viridis, plasma, inferno, magma, cividis, gray, coolwarm, RdBu (and _r): the 256-entry tables are generated from matplotlib, and an independent fixture of 1008 samples per map (including the ends and out-of-range values) is compared as floats and as bytes; the test also checks that all 256 entries were sampled. Named colours and the cycle all 148 CSS4, 10 tab:, 8 single-letter colours, C0–C9, grey levels, short and long hex: exact.
data.layout#Layout: what how it is checked Layout testdata/layout.json: 15 kinds of figure at two sizes — line, bar, barh, hist, imshow, imshow + colorbar, scatter, log-log, fill + errorbar, contourf, 2x2 grid, twinx, offsets, axhline/axvline, inverted and singular limits: every Axes position (after aspect and colorbar) and view limits (after margins and sticky edges) to 1e-9 relative, and every tick label and offset text exactly. TightLayout matplotlib’s _auto_adjust_subplotpars, ported; testdata/layout.json holds matplotlib’s positions after fig.tight_layout() for 6 kinds of figure at two sizes (single Axes, labelled, 2x2 labelled, twinx with two labels, offsets, log-log). Every Axes edge is within 0.005 of the figure (worst measured 0.0049, 2.4 pixels): the algorithm is the same, the measured width of text is not — matplotlib’s is FreeType’s hinted box, every glyph a whole number of pixels; go-plot’s is the string’s advance. Defaults figure 6.4 x 4.8 in at 100 dpi, subplot parameters, font sizes, tick sizes and pads, line widths, marker sizes, dash patterns (scaled by line width), patch and grid colours, legend geometry, colorbar fraction/pad/aspect: transcribed from matplotlibrc and checked by the rendering comparison below.
data.negative-controls#Negative controls:
A comparison that cannot fail proves nothing. Two deliberately perturbed go-plot figures are compared with matplotlib’s line, and both must fail:
line_shifted, the x limits widened by 0.1 data units at the left: tick error 4 px, overlap 0.436; line_1px, the view slid by 0.03 data units, 1.35 pixels: tick error 2 px, overlap 0.779. Both are caught; the smaller one by the tick detector and by the overlap, so a one-pixel slip of the data does not pass.
data.rendering-comparison#Rendering compariso:
tools/compare draws twelve reference figures with go-plot and with matplotlib — same data, size and dpi — and measures each pair with one detector applied to both images: the axes frames (columns and rows of long dark runs), the tick marks (dark for the three pixels just outside each bottom and left spine, within the frame), and the pixels of the first cycle colour inside the frames. Tolerances: frame and ticks within 1 pixel, C0 pixel count within 10 %, overlap of C0 pixels (each side dilated by 1 pixel) at least 0.90.
figure frames ticks (go / mpl) tick error C0 pixels (go / mpl) overlap mean abs diff (0–255) line equal 15 / 15 0 px 1695 / 1736 1.000 1.01 scatter + colorbar equal 11 / 11 0 px – – 0.53 bars (1x2) equal 26 / 26 0 px 76024 / 76034 1.000 0.67 hist equal 17 / 17 0 px 49515 / 49515 1.000 0.63 imshow + colorbar equal 16 / 16 0 px 38429 / 38683 1.000 0.77 contourf + contour + colorbar equal 16 / 16 0 px – – 0.75 log-log with grid equal 11 / 11 0 px 770 / 775 1.000 0.64 errorbar, fill, axhline/axvline, text, annotate equal 14 / 14 0 px 1688 / 1558 0.994 1.03 twinx equal 11 / 11 0 px 881 / 891 1.000 0.94 2x2 grid, offsets equal 41 / 41 0 px 4991 / 4944 0.997 1.79 int32 ndarray with markers equal 14 / 14 0 px 2380 / 2465 1.000 0.32 1000² imshow (perf figure) equal 10 / 10 0 px 17426 / 17629 1.000 1.59 2x2 labelled, TightLayout ±2 px 14 / 14 2 px 713 / 700 0.970 6.71 1e6-point line (perf figure) equal 13 / 13 0 px 12032 / 15405 1.000 2.07 In twelve of the fourteen, every frame lands on the same pixel rows and columns and every tick on the same pixel. The images were also looked at, side by side.
Two fail the tolerances, and are reported rather than loosened:
TightLayout: frames and ticks within 2 pixels, not 1, for the reason given above — the width of tick labels, which tight layout makes room for, is measured differently. Side by side the figures are not distinguishable by eye. The dense line: go-plot paints 22 % fewer saturated C0 pixels. Every go-plot pixel is within one pixel of a matplotlib one (overlap 1.000); the difference is how dark the edges of a stroke that crosses itself thousands of times come out — Agg’s scanline accumulates such a stroke differently from go-gfx’s coverage sweep. It is not the simplification: drawn without it, go-plot’s count changes by 0.3 %, while matplotlib’s own simplified and unsimplified renderings differ by 9 %.

git clone https://github.com/go-plot/plot && cd plot go test ./... # includes the matplotlib fixtures uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy python tools/gen_ticks.py # regenerate a fixture cd tools/compare && go run . -out DIR && uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy python figures.py DIR \ && uv run --with matplotlib --with numpy python compare.py DIR line=line ... Write rendered images to a directory outside the repository.
What does not equal matplotlib is on Differences.
data.ticks#Ticks: what how it is checked Tick locations, labels, offset text on linear and log axes ticker/testdata/ticks.json: 408 axes of real figures (4 sizes, 37 linear and 14 log ranges, x and y): every location bit for bit, every label and offset character for character, minor log ticks and their labels included. Locator and formatter parameters a default figure never uses ticker/testdata/units.json: 45 MaxNLocator (nbins, steps, integer, symmetric, prune, min_n_ticks), 42 LogLocator (base 2, e, 10; subs list/auto/all; numticks), 72 ScalarFormatter (math text, no offset, fixed power limits, no scientific, ASCII minus, one or no location), 25 LogFormatterSciNotation, nonsingular, and %g. Exact, except base-e log locations, compared to 1e-15: NumPy’s e**n and Go’s math.Pow(e, n) differ in the last bit.

data.a-first-figure#A first figure:
This is the example of go-plot’s README. It plots a sine as a line, then the same points as markers, labels the x axis with some TeX, adds a legend, and writes a PNG to standard output:
package main import ( "math" "os" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func main() { x := make([]float64, 200) y := make([]float64, 200) for i := range x { x[i] = float64(i) / 20 y[i] = math.Sin(x[i]) } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Label(`$\sin t$`)) ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Marker("o"), plot.LineStyle("None"), plot.MarkerSize(2)) ax.SetXLabel(`time $t$ (s)`) ax.Legend() fig.SavePNG(os.Stdout) } go run . > sine.png The same figure, saved with SaveSVG instead:
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("quickstart", quickstart) } // The README's example, with SaveSVG in place of SavePNG. func quickstart() *plot.Figure { x := make([]float64, 200) y := make([]float64, 200) for i := range x { x[i] = float64(i) / 20 y[i] = math.Sin(x[i]) } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Label(`$\sin t$`)) ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Marker("o"), plot.LineStyle("None"), plot.MarkerSize(2)) ax.SetXLabel(`time $t$ (s)`) ax.Legend() return fig } Read it as matplotlib:
go-plot matplotlib fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 1, squeeze=False) ax := axs[0][0] ax = axs[0][0] ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Label(...)) ax.plot(x, y, label=...) plot.Marker("o"), plot.LineStyle("None"), plot.MarkerSize(2) marker="o", linestyle="None", markersize=2 ax.SetXLabel(...) ax.set_xlabel(...) ax.Legend() ax.legend() fig.SavePNG(w), fig.SaveSVG(w) fig.savefig(f, format="png"), format="svg" The figure is matplotlib’s default: 6.4 × 4.8 inches at 100 dpi, so 640 × 480 pixels, with the tab10 colour cycle (the line is C0, the markers C1). plot.FigSize(w, h) and plot.DPI(d) change it:
fig, axs := plot.Subplots(2, 2, plot.FigSize(8, 6), plot.DPI(150))
data.data#Data: Data arguments take []float64, []float32, []int, []int32, []int64, a scalar, or a *ndarray.Array of any of go-ndarray’s dtypes. A type that cannot be plotted, or x and y of different lengths, panics: both are programming errors, as an index out of range is. See the API.
data.in-a-notebook#In a notebook: fig.Display() returns the figure in every format a notebook front end may show, keyed by MIME type: image/svg+xml and image/png. It is the display contract of the go-notebook kernel, so a cell whose last expression is a figure shows it; it is the notebook’s plt.show().
data.install#Install: go get github.com/go-plot/plot@v0.2.0 Go 1.27.2 or later. Nothing else: no Python, no C library, no font to install. The fonts (DejaVu Sans for text, STIX Two Math for TeX) are compiled in.

data:
Two figures, each saved as PNG and as SVG, at matplotlib’s default size (6.4 x 4.8 in, 100 dpi):
line: Plot of a 1,000,000-point random walk; imshow: Imshow of a 1000 x 1000 array (sin(i/37)·cos(j/23)), viridis.
data.method#Method:
tools/compare/perf.py (driving tools/compare/perf/main.go):
both sides build the same data, with the same generator, before the clock starts; the clock covers creating the figure, plotting, and writing the file to memory; every measurement is a fresh process on both sides (so neither keeps a warm glyph or path cache the other lacks), and the two are interleaved case by case, run by run, so that load changes on the host hit both alike; 9 runs per case; the tables give medians, with the spread. What is not in the numbers: Python’s interpreter start and import matplotlib.pyplot (about half a second on this machine), and the Go process start (a few milliseconds). A notebook keeps both warm, so the in-process time is the comparable one.
Host: Apple M4 Max, 16 cores, macOS; Go 1.27.2; Python 3.12.12, matplotlib 3.11.2, NumPy 2.5.3, Agg backend. The host was shared and loaded: load average 22.6 before the run and 21.7 after it, on 16 cores. Absolute times are therefore pessimistic for both; the interleaving is what keeps the ratio fair. Measured 2026-10-10.

data.where-the-time-goes-and-what-changed-to-:
The first measurement of the line PNG was 0.124 s, half matplotlib’s speed. Profiling (go test -bench -cpuprofile) showed three costs, each now fixed:
the data limits of the million points were recomputed per axis per draw (0.67 s of 2.2 s sampled): they are now taken once, when the artist is added; the coverage sweep of go-gfx’s rasteriser sorts each scanline’s crossings by insertion, quadratic in the crossings, and a dense polyline has thousands per scanline: strokes of more than 512 segments are now rasterised in 512-segment pieces (matplotlib has the same knob, agg.path.chunksize, off by default), whose seams are round joins, so the only visible change is that the line’s own two ends are round rather than projecting; STIX Two Math (for TeX labels) was parsed on every figure: it is now parsed only when a label contains TeX. Like matplotlib, go-plot simplifies dense lines before drawing them (matplotlib’s PathSimplifier, ported): the 1e6-point walk is drawn as 11,738 vertices. That is why the SVG of a million points is about 220 kB on both sides.

Each figure on this page was drawn by go-plot v0.2.0 from the code below it. The code is not a copy: the page reads it from figures/ in this site’s repository, where go run . draws every image, and the CI draws them again and fails if any differs from the one shown. linspace is a helper in figures/main.go, numpy.linspace’s equivalent.

data.a-grid-with-tightlayout#A grid, with Tig:
Subplots(rows, cols) lays out a grid with matplotlib’s subplot parameters; TightLayout then moves the Axes so that titles and labels do not overlap.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("grid", grid) } func grid() *plot.Figure { x := linspace(0, 1, 200) fig, axs := plot.Subplots(2, 2) for r := range 2 { for c := range 2 { k := float64(1 + 2*r + c) y := make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { y[i] = math.Sin(2*math.Pi*k*v) * math.Exp(-k*v) } ax := axs[r][c] ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Color("C"+string(rune('0'+2*r+c)))) ax.SetTitle(`$k = ` + string(rune('0'+int(k))) + `$`) ax.SetXLabel("x") ax.SetYLabel(`$\sin(2\pi k x)\,e^{-kx}$`) } } fig.TightLayout() return fig }
data.bars#Bars:
Bar draws bars 0.8 wide, centred on x, from 0; Width and an x offset put two series side by side. Barh is the horizontal form, and Colors gives one colour per bar.
package main import "github.com/go-plot/plot" func init() { register("bars", bars) } func bars() *plot.Figure { x := []float64{0, 1, 2, 3, 4} a := []float64{3, 7, 5, 9, 4} b := []float64{2, 4, 6, 3, 5} fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 2, plot.FigSize(8, 3.6)) left, right := axs[0][0], axs[0][1] left.Bar(x, a, plot.Width(0.4), plot.Label("a")) shifted := make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { shifted[i] = v + 0.4 } left.Bar(shifted, b, plot.Width(0.4), plot.Label("b")) left.SetXTicks([]float64{0.2, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2, 4.2}, "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri") left.SetTitle("Bar") left.Legend() right.Barh(x, a, plot.Colors("C0", "C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")) right.SetTitle("Barh, one colour per bar") fig.TightLayout() return fig }
data.contours#Contours:
Contour draws iso-lines and Contourf fills the bands between them, at levels chosen as matplotlib chooses them (ContourSet._autolev). x and y give the column and row coordinates.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("contour", contour) } func contour() *plot.Figure { x, y := linspace(-3, 3, 61), linspace(-2, 2, 41) z := make([][]float64, len(y)) for i, v := range y { z[i] = make([]float64, len(x)) for j, u := range x { z[i][j] = (1-u/2+math.Pow(u, 5)+math.Pow(v, 3))*math.Exp(-u*u-v*v) } } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] m := ax.Contourf(x, y, z, plot.NLevels(10), plot.Cmap("RdBu_r")) ax.Contour(x, y, z, plot.NLevels(10), plot.Color("k"), plot.LineWidth(0.5)) fig.Colorbar(m, ax) ax.SetTitle("Contourf and Contour") return fig }
data.error-bars-bands-and-annotations#Error b: package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("errorbar", errorbar) } func errorbar() *plot.Figure { x := linspace(0, 10, 11) y, e := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { y[i] = 2 + math.Sin(v/2) e[i] = 0.1 + 0.03*v } lo, hi := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x)) for i := range x { lo[i], hi[i] = y[i]-2*e[i], y[i]+2*e[i] } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.FillBetween(x, lo, hi, plot.Alpha(0.2), plot.Label(`$\pm 2\sigma$`)) ax.ErrorBar(x, y, plot.YErr(e), plot.CapSize(3), plot.Marker("o"), plot.Label(`measured $\pm\sigma$`)) ax.Axhline(2, plot.Color("gray"), plot.LineStyle("--"), plot.LineWidth(1)) ax.Annotate("baseline", 8, 2, 6.5, 1.3, plot.Arrow()) ax.SetTitle("ErrorBar, FillBetween, Axhline, Annotate") ax.Legend(plot.Loc("upper left")) return fig }
data.histograms#Histograms:
Hist bins with NumPy’s algorithm: 10 equal bins over the data range by default, Bins(n) for n, BinEdges for explicit edges, Density to normalise.
package main import ( "math" "math/rand/v2" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("hist", hist) } func hist() *plot.Figure { rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2)) a, b := make([]float64, 5000), make([]float64, 5000) for i := range a { a[i] = rng.NormFloat64() b[i] = 1.5 + 0.6*rng.NormFloat64() } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Hist(a, plot.Bins(40), plot.Density(), plot.Alpha(0.6), plot.Label(`$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$`)) ax.Hist(b, plot.Bins(40), plot.Density(), plot.Alpha(0.6), plot.Label(`$\mathcal{N}(1.5, 0.6^2)$`)) x := linspace(-4, 4, 200) pdf := make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { pdf[i] = math.Exp(-v*v/2) / math.Sqrt(2*math.Pi) } ax.Plot(x, pdf, plot.Color("k"), plot.LineWidth(1), plot.Label("density of the first")) ax.SetTitle("Hist with 40 bins, normalised") ax.Legend() return fig }
data.images#Images:
Imshow colours 2-D data through a colormap (viridis by default), with pixel centres at integer coordinates and row 0 at the top; a 3-D array of shape (rows, cols, 3 or 4) is shown as RGB(A). Here the data is a go-ndarray array.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-ndarray/ndarray" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("imshow", imshow) } func imshow() *plot.Figure { const rows, cols = 120, 160 data := make([]float64, rows*cols) for i := range rows { for j := range cols { data[i*cols+j] = math.Sin(float64(i)/11) * math.Cos(float64(j)/17) } } z, err := ndarray.FromSlice(data, rows, cols) if err != nil { panic(err) } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] m := ax.Imshow(z, plot.Cmap("viridis")) fig.Colorbar(m, ax) ax.SetTitle(`Imshow of a $120 \times 160$ ndarray`) return fig }
data.lines-and-markers#Lines and markers:
Plot draws a line in the next colour of the cycle. LineStyle takes "-", "--", "-.", ":" (and "None"); Marker takes matplotlib’s marker codes.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("lines", lines) } func lines() *plot.Figure { x := linspace(0, 2*math.Pi, 40) styles := []string{"-", "--", "-.", ":"} markers := []string{"o", "s", "^", "D"} fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] for k := range styles { y := make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { y[i] = math.Sin(v + float64(k)*math.Pi/4) } ax.Plot(x, y, plot.LineStyle(styles[k]), plot.Marker(markers[k]), plot.MarkerSize(4), plot.Label(`style "`+styles[k]+`", marker "`+markers[k]+`"`)) } ax.SetTitle("Line styles and markers, colours from the cycle") ax.SetYLim(-2, 1.2) ax.Legend(plot.Loc("lower center"), plot.FontSize(8)) return fig }
data.log-scales#Log scales:
SetXScale("log") and SetYScale("log") use matplotlib’s LogLocator and LogFormatterSciNotation, so the decades and their labels are matplotlib’s.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("loglog", loglog) } func loglog() *plot.Figure { n := linspace(1, 6, 26) x := make([]float64, len(n)) for i, e := range n { x[i] = math.Pow(10, e) } lin, nlogn, sq := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { lin[i], nlogn[i], sq[i] = v, v*math.Log2(v), v*v } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(x, lin, plot.Label(`$n$`)) ax.Plot(x, nlogn, plot.Label(`$n \log_2 n$`)) ax.Plot(x, sq, plot.Label(`$n^2$`)) ax.SetXScale("log") ax.SetYScale("log") ax.Grid(true) ax.SetXLabel(`$n$`) ax.SetYLabel("operations") ax.SetTitle("Log scales: LogLocator and LogFormatterSciNotation") ax.Legend() return fig }
data.pie-and-donut#Pie and donut:
Pie is matplotlib’s ax.pie.
Wedge i covers x[i]/sum(x) of a turn, from 3 o’clock counter-clockwise, in the colours of the cycle. Labels sit at 1.1 radii, and AutoPct percentages at 0.6. The Axes gets an equal aspect, no frame and no ticks. The judge against matplotlib compares every wedge path vertex by vertex, every label’s position and alignment, the Axes box, and ≥ 99% of the pixels. Sizes that are negative, NaN, infinite or all zero return an error (ErrPieNegative, ErrPieNonFinite, ErrPieZero) and draw nothing, as matplotlib raises.
Donut(x, width) is a ring, with the percentages in its middle. Two go-plot options matter for data-driven charts:
PlainText() sets the labels as they are, with no TeX: “$5” is a dollar. SpreadLabels() moves the labels of thin wedges apart, with leader lines. StartAngle(90), CounterClock(false) starts at 12 o’clock and runs clockwise, as go-widgets/toolkit’s interactive PieChart does. Colors(colors.Tableau10...) gives the toolkit’s palette.
package main import "github.com/go-plot/plot" func init() { register("pie", pie) } func pie() *plot.Figure { spend := []float64{42, 27, 18, 13} names := []string{"Salaries", "Rent", "Travel", "Other"} fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 2, plot.FigSize(8, 4)) left, right := axs[0][0], axs[0][1] if err := left.Pie(spend, plot.Labels(names...), plot.AutoPct("%1.1f%%"), plot.PlainText(), plot.Explode(0.05, 0, 0, 0)); err != nil { panic(err) } left.SetTitle("Pie") if err := right.Donut(spend, 0.35, plot.Labels(names...), plot.AutoPct("%.0f%%"), plot.PlainText(), plot.EdgeColor("w"), plot.StartAngle(90), plot.CounterClock(false)); err != nil { panic(err) } right.SetTitle("Donut, from 12 o'clock, clockwise") return fig }
data.scatter#Scatter:
With CValues, colours come from a colormap and Scatter returns a *Mappable for Colorbar. Sizes gives each point its area in points².
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("scatter", scatter) } func scatter() *plot.Figure { n := 120 x, y := make([]float64, n), make([]float64, n) c, s := make([]float64, n), make([]float64, n) for i := range n { t := float64(i) / float64(n) * 6 * math.Pi r := 1 + t/4 x[i], y[i] = r*math.Cos(t), r*math.Sin(t) c[i] = t s[i] = 10 + 4*t } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] m := ax.Scatter(x, y, plot.CValues(c), plot.Sizes(s), plot.Cmap("plasma"), plot.Alpha(0.8)) ax.SetAspect(1) ax.SetTitle("Scatter: size and colour per point") fig.Colorbar(m, ax).SetYLabel(`angle $\theta$ (rad)`) return fig }
data.two-y-axes#Two y axes:
TwinX returns a new Axes sharing the x axis, with its y axis on the right and its own colour cycle.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("twinx", twinx) } func twinx() *plot.Figure { t := linspace(0, 24, 97) temp, hum := make([]float64, len(t)), make([]float64, len(t)) for i, v := range t { temp[i] = 14 + 6*math.Sin((v-9)*math.Pi/12) hum[i] = 70 - 15*math.Sin((v-9)*math.Pi/12) } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(t, temp, plot.Color("C3")) ax.SetXLabel("hour") ax.SetYLabel("temperature (°C)") right := ax.TwinX() right.Plot(t, hum, plot.Color("C0"), plot.LineStyle("--")) right.SetYLabel("relative humidity (%)") ax.SetTitle("TwinX: two y axes on one x axis") return fig }

data:
Any string go-plot draws — a title, an axis label, a legend entry, a colorbar label, Text, Annotate — may contain TeX math between dollar signs:
ax.SetXLabel(`time $t$ (s)`) ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Label(`$e^{-t/4}\cos 2t$`)) Use Go’s raw strings (backquotes), so that backslashes reach TeX unescaped.
data.a-tex-typesetter-not-mathtext#A TeX type:
matplotlib sets $...$ with mathtext, its own approximation of TeX. go-plot sets it with go-tex/math, a real TeX math typesetter using the OpenType MATH table of STIX Two Math: fractions, radicals, big operators, limits, matrices and \left...\right are laid out as TeX lays them out, which mathtext only approximates. go-tex/math’s output is parsed back into paths and scaled to the label’s size, so TeX is drawn as outlines in both PNG and SVG and needs no font installed.
package main import ( "math" "github.com/go-plot/plot" ) func init() { register("tex", tex) } func tex() *plot.Figure { x := linspace(-4, 4, 400) y := make([]float64, len(x)) for i, v := range x { y[i] = math.Exp(-v*v/2) / math.Sqrt(2*math.Pi) } fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1) ax := axs[0][0] ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Label(`$\varphi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-x^2/2}$`)) ax.FillBetween(x, y, nil, plot.Where(between(x, -1, 1)), plot.Alpha(0.3)) ax.Text(1.4, 0.25, `$\int_{-1}^{1} \varphi(x)\,dx \approx 0.683$`, plot.FontSize(12)) ax.SetTitle(`The standard normal density $\varphi$`) ax.SetXLabel(`$x$`) ax.SetYLabel(`$\varphi(x)$`) ax.Legend(plot.Loc("upper left")) return fig } func between(x []float64, lo, hi float64) []bool { m := make([]bool, len(x)) for i, v := range x { m[i] = v >= lo && v <= hi } return m }
data.cost#Cost: STIX Two Math is parsed only when a label contains TeX: a figure without any does not pay for it (performance).
data.plain-text#Plain text: Text outside dollar signs is set in DejaVu Sans, matplotlib’s default font, from go-opentype/fonts, with kerning from DejaVu’s GPOS and kern tables. Glyphs are drawn as filled outlines, so rotated labels and SVG output need no font. Positions follow matplotlib’s Text._get_layout (line metrics from the OS/2 table, alignment, rotation, anchoring), and like Agg the pen is put on a whole pixel. How the pixels of text differ from matplotlib’s is on Differences.
data.replacing-the-renderer#Replacing the ren: Figure.Text is a text.Renderer with two methods, Layout(s, size) and LineMetrics(size). Setting another one changes the fonts of the whole figure.
data.tick-labels-keep-matplotlibs-look#Tick l: The one exception is \mathdefault{...}, which is what matplotlib’s tick formatters emit (10^{3}, 2\times10^{1}). It is set in DejaVu Sans with mathtext’s own superscript rules (shift = max(sup1 · x-height, depth + x-height/4), scripts at 0.7 size), so tick labels match matplotlib’s look and position. The decades on the log-log figure are set this way.
